answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in Emma (1815): Emma thinks this to herself while reflecting on Harriet Smith’s warmth of character, in Volume II, Chapter XIII (continuous Chapter 31).

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: “There is no charm equal to tenderness of heart,” said she afterwards to herself. “There is nothing to be compared to it. Warmth and tenderness of heart, with an affectionate, open manner, will beat all the clearness of head in the world, for attraction, I am sure it will. It is tenderness of heart which makes my dear father so generally beloved—which gives Isabella all her popularity.—I have it not—but I know how to prize and respect it.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line occurs as Emma Woodhouse’s private reflection after a scene with her friend Harriet Smith. Having just witnessed Harriet’s open-hearted, guileless affection, Emma contrasts it with her own more analytical temperament and concludes that “warmth and tenderness of heart, with an affectionate, open manner, will beat all the clearness of head in the world, for attraction.”

It is one of the novel’s clearest statements of its recurring theme: that Emma, for all her wit and self-assurance, still has emotional growing to do — and that she recognizes, even if she cannot yet fully embody, the virtue of tenderness in others.
